paragraphs.text: A study at Brenner University followed 120 secondary school students for a term, recording their sleep with wristbands and comparing it with their test results. Students who slept at least eight hours on school nights scored, on average, 7 per cent higher in mathematics than those who slept less than seven.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: The researchers were careful not to claim that sleep alone caused the difference. Students who slept longer also tended to have more regular routines and to spend less time on their phones in the evening, and either factor might affect results.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: One finding was clearer. Students who caught up on sleep at weekends did not perform better than those who slept little throughout the week. A long lie-in on Saturday, the authors conclude, cannot undo the effects of five short nights.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The team recommends that schools teach students about sleep in the same way they teach about diet and exercise. They also suggest that homework deadlines should not be set for late evening, since many students stay up to meet them.
paragraphs.label: D
